title: Snowflake shapes arise from growth inhibition captured by a hexagonal cellular automaton

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Snowflake shapes arise from growth inhibition captured by a hexagonal cellular automaton

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The main features of snowflake shapes are reproduced by a hexagonal cellular automaton in which a cell becomes ice only if exactly one neighbor is ice, which represents the inhibition of nearby growth by released latent heat.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: One can capture this basic effect by having a cellular automaton with rules in which cells become black if they have exactly one black neighbor, but stay white whenever they have more than one black neighbor.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 8, “Implications for Everyday Systems”; section “The Growth of Crystals” (from p. 369), p. 370. Scope: growth of snowflakes (ice crystals from water vapor)

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch08-02: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.56

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The cellular automaton is straightforward to simulate and snow-crystal images permit morphology comparison. Existing public imagery is less suitable for testing the proposed latent-heat mechanism, and shape fit has limited discrimination among rival crystal-growth models. Thus only the phenomenological part is currently approachable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare preregistered geometric descriptors of time-resolved snow-crystal images with outputs from the exact hexagonal rule and rival diffusion and heat-transport models. Support requires reproduction of the main descriptors plus an observed relation between local latent-heat conditions and growth suppression; visual similarity alone is insufficient.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Many distinct growth mechanisms can produce similar hexagonal morphology.

Main features is underspecified.

Archival final images lack local temperature and vapor histories.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Public snowflake images and a one-page simulation are enough to test whether this specific rule reproduces measured habit classes. The rule's lack of dependence on the conditions that organize the Nakaya diagram is a discriminator, not merely a difference of taste. Even so, several continuum and lattice models produce similar dendrites, so a picture match would not establish this cellular automaton as the mechanism.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Run the hexagonal exactly-one-neighbor cellular automaton and compare quantitative shape descriptors (branching order, facet-to-dendrite sequence, sixfold symmetry) with photographed snowflakes grown at known temperature and humidity. A match across the observed morphology diagram, better than rival growth models, would support the claim; systematic misses, especially the absence of temperature dependence, would refute it as an account of the main features.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The rule has no temperature or humidity parameter, while real snowflake habit is controlled by both.

Visual resemblance is shared by several dendritic models and does not by itself identify latent-heat inhibition.
